summary: This work establishes a high-throughput methodology to correlate two-level system (TLS) density in Al/AlOx/Al Josephson junctions with fabrication parameters and microstructure using 6,000 junctions and 600+ STEM images. A two-thirds reduction in TLS density ($\rho_{\mathrm{TLS}}$: from $0.20 \pm 0.10$ to $0.07 \pm 0.04$ GHz$^{-1}$ µm$^{-2}$) is achieved by increasing Al electrode thickness, which correlates with larger grain size (128 nm versus 40–60 nm) and reduced grain boundary density.
motivation: Strongly-coupled TLS in Josephson junctions limit qubit coherence and reliability, but their microscopic origins remain poorly understood and current mitigation strategies (thermal cycling, strain, electric fields) are complex and unscalable. Establishing direct correlations between fabrication, microstructure, and TLS density could enable predictive control through improved fabrication methods.
method: An automated resonator spectroscopy workflow detected 393 distinct TLS across five samples via residual-peak identification; an empirical Bayesian framework with calibrated false-positive and false-negative rates inferred TLS densities. Cross-sectional STEM imaging extracted electrode thickness, grain size, and roughness metrics across 709 images, which were statistically linked to TLS density via Pearson correlation and ridge regression.
result: Thicker Al electrodes (bottom 100 nm, top 150 nm) reduced mean TLS density by two-thirds compared to standard devices, with statistical significance ($p \le 0.05$, Kruskal–Wallis). Mean electrode thickness and grain size showed statistically significant correlations with reduced $\rho_{\mathrm{TLS}}$, with permutation importance identifying mean thickness as the primary predictor.
